tip: You can drop 'wenn' and lead with the verb: 'Hätten wir angefangen' means the same as 'Wenn wir angefangen hätten'.
'Wie komme ich zum ...?' is the standard way to ask for directions in German.
'Um ... zu' plus an infinitive expresses purpose: 'um fit zu bleiben' means in order to stay fit.
'Wenn es nach mir ginge' is a set phrase for 'if it were up to me', not a literal 'if it goes'.
In reported speech German uses a special verb form: 'seien' (not 'sind') signals these are her words, not stated fact.
'Statt' plus a 'zu'-infinitive means instead of doing something: 'statt mit dem Auto zu fahren' = instead of driving.
'Ohne ... zu' means without doing something: 'ohne zu frühstücken' = without having breakfast.
'Raten' takes a dative person: 'ich rate dir', not 'ich rate dich'.
'Geschweige denn' = let alone, naming a less likely thing after a negative: 'nicht angerufen, geschweige denn ... geschrieben'.
German can pack a whole phrase between article and noun: 'der im ganzen Land bekannte Schauspieler' = the actor known nationwide.
'Laut' (according to) takes the dative: 'laut dem Bericht', not 'laut den Bericht'.
'Gratulieren zu' + dative = to congratulate on: 'wir gratulieren dir ... zu deinem'.
Separable verbs split: 'ausmachen' becomes 'machen ... aus', with the prefix moving to the end: 'machen das Licht aus'.
'Sowohl ... als auch' means both ... and, and usually takes a plural verb: 'sowohl mein Bruder als auch meine Schwester studieren'.
'Sich entschuldigen' uses 'bei' for the person and 'für' for the reason: 'sich bei ihrem Nachbarn für den ... Lärm entschuldigt'.
'Weder ... noch' means neither ... nor; with two singular subjects the verb usually stays singular: 'der Mieter will'.
'Sich freuen auf' + accusative = to look forward to (a future event): 'auf unseren gemeinsamen Urlaub'.
'Sich anmelden für' + accusative = to sign up for: 'für den fortgeschrittenen Tanzkurs'.
'Anstatt' + 'zu'-infinitive = instead of doing something: 'anstatt in Panik zu geraten' = instead of panicking.
Separable verbs: 'zu' goes between prefix and stem, so 'ausgehen' becomes 'auszugehen'.
'Könnten Sie' is the softer, more polite version of 'Können Sie' for requests: 'Könnten Sie mir die Speisekarte bringen'.
'Ohne' + 'zu'-infinitive = without doing something: 'ohne lange nachzudenken' = without thinking for long.
Pair 'nicht nur' with 'sondern auch' for not only ... but also: 'nicht nur Deutsch gelernt, sondern auch Französisch'.
In 'je ... desto', the 'je' clause puts its verb last: 'Je weniger ich schlafe, desto schlechter konzentriere ich mich'.
'Sich freuen über' + accusative = to be happy about (a past or present event): 'über das wunderbare Geburtstagsgeschenk'.
In the perfect tense, 'lassen' plus another verb stays 'lassen', not 'gelassen': 'die Kinder ... spielen lassen'.
'Verlassen' alone means to leave or abandon, but 'sich verlassen auf' flips it: 'wir verlassen uns ... auf' = we rely on.
'Trotzdem' starts the clause here, so the verb comes before the subject: 'trotzdem half er', not 'trotzdem er half'.
'Träumen von' + dative = to dream of: 'von einer langen Reise'.
'Die Flinte ins Korn werfen' is a set idiom for giving up, nothing to do with a real 'Flinte' (shotgun) or 'Korn' (grain).
